title: Experimental quantum cryptography with single photons and imperfect devices
authors: Aodhán Corrigan, Koray Kaymazlar, Zhiyao Wang, Lucas Rickert, Daniel Vajner, Martin von Helversen, Hanqing Liu, Shulun Li, Haiqiao Ni, Zhichuan Niu, Devashish Tupkary, Tobias Heindel
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) allows for provably secure key distribution between two trusted parties. Because the security and performance of QKD protocols rely on devices that behave according to specific assumptions, idealized or inaccurate assumptions about device behavior can introduce security loopholes. Real devices can never be perfectly characterized, and their performance metrics are always subject to certain error margins, which must be accounted for in a rigorous theoretical analysis. Only recently have rigorous finite-size results allowed for imperfect characterizations of devices (where device parameter have uncertainty margins) - an advance yet to be considered in experimental implementations of the BB84 protocol. In this work, we prove the security and analyze the performance of an implementation of the BB84 protocol using single photons generated by a semiconductor quantum dot light source in combination with dynamic polarization-state encoding. We consider the presence of incompletely characterized devices by accounting for imperfections in the single-photon source (in terms of finite g(2)(0)) as well as the receiver (non-ideal beam-splitters, finite detector efficiencies, and dark counts), all with error margins. The resulting protocol implementation shows competitive performance, paving the way towards practical and loop-hole free implementations of QKD.
summary: This paper experimentally demonstrates a robust Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) system using single photons from semiconductor quantum dots. Crucially, it advances the field by providing rigorous security analysis that accounts for unavoidable imperfections in real-world components like sources and detectors. The results show competitive performance, paving the way for practical, loophole-free quantum communication.
main_problem: The primary challenge is rigorously proving the security of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols when using real-world devices whose performance cannot be perfectly characterized.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that a BB84 implementation using semiconductor quantum dots can achieve competitive, loophole-free performance by explicitly accounting for source imperfections and detector noise margins.
method: The work combines experimental measurement of key metrics (QBER, g^(2)(0)) with advanced theoretical security proofs that incorporate statistical bounds on unobservable quantities like the phase error rate.
model_or_system: The system is an experimental implementation of the BB84 protocol using single photons generated by a semiconductor quantum dot source and analyzed by superconducting nanowire single photon detectors (SNSPDs).
key_observables: Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) ($\approx 3.51\%$), second-order correlation function g^(2)(0), and the calculated secure key length in bits.
important_parameters: Source mean photon number ($\mu = 0.005$), detector relative efficiencies ($\vec{\eta}$), and error margins associated with device imperfections.
main_assumptions: The security analysis relies on recent theoretical advances that allow for imperfect characterization of devices, modeling the real source via Source Map arguments.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (BB84 diagram), confirm single-photon emission statistics using g^(2)(2) histograms, and compare simulated vs. measured key rates considering device imperfections.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need to address device loopholes in QKD security proofs, detailing the physical implementation using QD sources, presenting measurements of performance metrics (QBER), and concluding with a rigorous analysis bounding the achievable secure key rate under realistic noise models.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete bridge between theoretical quantum information security proofs and practical experimental realization, which is crucial for advancing photonic quantum communication technologies.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Experimental setup for our BB84 implementation. Alice prepares single photons using a deterministic single photon source comprised of a single QD embedded in a photonic microcavity and dynamically selects the polarization using an EOM. These are sent to Bob’s passive four-state polarization analyzer, comprised of SNSPD based detectors.

FIG. 2. a) Emission spectrum of the QD microcavity device under quasi-resonant (p-shell) excitation. The strongly Purcell- enhanced trion state (X+) at 920.1 nm exhibits a ultra-fast decay time < 50 ps, as depicted in the time-resolved measurement in the inset. b) Second-order photon correlation histogram measured in Hanbury-Brown and Twiss configuration. The strong multiphoton suppression of g(2)(τ = 0) = (1.7 ± 0.5) · 10−2 demonstrates sub-Poissonian emission statistics.

FIG. 3. (a) Example of the employed random sequence for a 200 ns long excerpt containing 16 bits of given voltage level U in the four polarization states, followed immediately by the binary switching in each bit as inspired by the Manchester encoding. (b) Sample of time-tags averaged over multiple QRNG sequence loops, showing high polarization suppression in all four bases over ∼400 ns of the QRNG sequence. (c) Maximum tolerable QBER of 11% for BB84 QKD and achieved QBER for Z and X bases over the course of the experiment (i.e. 20 mins), with a time average of 3.51%.

FIG. 4. Simulated key rate plot for experimental parameters, as well as key rate computed from experimental run. Simulation is performed by using error rate observed in experiment, but changing loss. Computed with sampling parameters εPNE = εa = εb = ε0 = εAT,Z = 10−9 (See Appendix A for details), postprocessing parameters εPA = εEV = 10−9, and probability of Z rounds used for eZ estimation of 1%. Horizontal axis begins at 0, assuming lossless components. Note accounting for imperfections drastically reduces key rate by nearly an order of magnitude, although further refinements of proof techniques will likely be able to decrease this impact.

FIG. 5. (a): Measured (raw) second order autocorrelation g(2)(τ)-histogram of the employed QD emitter. (b) Blinking-corrected g(2)(τ)-histogram by dividing the data in (a) by Eq. B1 for the paramters listed in Tab III.
